Court of Queen
’
s Bench of Alberta

Citation:
Chohan v. Cadsky, 2007 ABQB 498

Date:

20070727

Docket:

0403 18975

Registry:

Edmonton

Between:

Inderjit Singh Chohan

Plaintiff

-
and -

Otakar Cadsky, Larry Ohlhauser, Capital
Health Authority,

Kenneth Gardener, Glen Baker, the
University

of Alberta and Kelay Ohlhauser

Defendants

_______________________________________________________

Reasons for Judgment

of
the

Honourable Mr. Justice E.S. Lefsrud

_______________________________________________________

The Claim

[
1
]

Dr. Inderjit Singh Chohan is a forensic psychiatrist who at all relevant
times worked, and continues to work, at the Forensic Assessment and Community
Services (“FACS”), the outpatient component of Alberta Hospital Edmonton
(“AHE”).

[
2
]

The central allegation to Dr. Chohan’s
claim is that around February 4, 2003, Dr. Otakar Cadsky, also a forensic
psychiatrist and clinical coordinator at FACS for some time, defamed Dr. Chohan
by referring to him a “paranoid Sikh” in a conversation with two colleagues,
Drs. Rai and Woods. Dr. Chohan also alleges that Dr. Cadsky stated it was his
intention to force Dr. Chohan to resign from his position within FACS. Further,

Dr. Chohan generally alleges that all of the Defendants made various
defamatory comments, and that starting in February 2003, they commenced a
course of action to defame and discredit him, thereby causing damage to his reputation
and exposing him to hatred, ridicule, scorn and contempt.

[
3
]

These alleged facts are not
complex. However, they take place against quite a particular backdrop.

[
4
]

First, Dr. Cadsky had previously
been the subject of some disciplinary action as a result of his reference to a
Jewish psychiatrist from Calgary as a “greedy money grubbing Jew”.

[
5
]

Secondly, around the time of the
alleged statements and Dr. Cadsky’s official reinstatement as clinical
coordinator at the end of March 2003, Capital Health was taking over
responsibility for FACS from the Alberta Mental Health Board (effective April
1, 2003).

[
6
]

Thirdly, there were two fairly
distinct factions of psychiatrists within FACS and AHE; Dr. Chohan is
identified in the evidence as being part of the “new guard” and Dr. Cadsky part
of the “old guard”.

[
7
]

Fourthly, the comments made by Dr.
Cadsky were made at his home over a glass of wine to his colleagues, Drs. Rai
and Woods, who had dropped by for a visit. Dr. Cadsky was on stress leave at
the time, having lost his 14 year old daughter to Hodgkins’ disease in early
December 2002, having suffered a heart attack and bypass surgery two weeks
later, and having undergone the break up of his marriage around the same time.

[
8
]

Fifthly, although Dr. Chohan was
told about these comments, he felt unable to make specific reference to them
for a considerable length of time, due to a concern over potential
repercussions on Dr. Rai’s employment status. This resulted in considerable
frustration on Dr. Chohan’s part as he tried to persuade various persons in
authority of the serious nature of his concerns.

[
9
]

Finally, a number of initiatives
were undertaken after February 2003 to heal the divisions within FACS,
including those relating to Dr. Chohan’s complaints; none was deemed
satisfactory by Dr. Chohan, and all precipitated further allegations by him of
defamation and intimidation.

[
10
]

The Court heard almost three full
weeks of evidence in this matter. What emerged is a picture of a very
dysfunctional working environment in which name calling, finger pointing,
intransigence and conspiratorial workings have thwarted the best intentions of
all of the psychiatrists involved to the point that a certain number of the
psychiatrists from both factions have left FACS, and a greater number have been
left significantly demoralized. How such a group of obviously intelligent
professionals could work themselves into such a state is beyond comprehension.
Fortunately, it is not for this Court to psychoanalyze the participants in this
drama, but simply to determine whether Dr. Chohan has made out his claim of
defamation.

The Defences

[
11
]

The original Defendants included The
University of Alberta and Kelay Ohlhauser. The action has been discontinued as
against those two Defendants.
The defences raised by the remaining
Defendants are as follows.

[
12
]

The Statement of Defence of Dr. Cadsky,
Capital Health and Dr. Kenneth Gardener denies that any statements made were
false or were made maliciously or recklessly without regard for the truth, and
further that any statements were made in the normal course of the discharge of
their duties and are subject to qualified privilege. It is admitted Dr. Cadsky
referred to Dr. Chohan as a “paranoid Sikh”, but this was not racially
motivated and was rather a “colloquial expression of fact” made in good faith
in circumstances which rendered it subject to qualified privilege. It is denied
that Dr. Cadsky stated it was his intention to force Dr. Chohan to resign from
his position.
Further, there were reasonable grounds for concerns about
Dr. Chohan’s mental health, and further (or alternatively) the statements made
were true. Finally, the Defendants state that if Dr. Chohan has suffered harm
to his personal and professional reputation, which these Defendants deny, it is
due to his own conduct.

[
13
]

The Statement of Defence of Dr. Larry
Ohlhauser states that he became involved in the situation due to a request by
psychiatrist
colleagues of Dr. Chohan who expressed concern over the latter’s mental health.
Dr. Ohlhauser contacted Dr. Hibbard, who it was suggested by the concerned
colleagues would be an appropriate psychiatrist to contact with respect to a
psychiatric assessment of Dr. Chohan. It is denied that Dr. Ohlhauser accused
Dr. Chohan of being paranoid, spread rumors regarding his mental health, or
commenced a course of action to defame or discredit Dr. Chohan. The statements
complained of were not defamatory, and no statements were made viciously or
recklessly without regard for the truth, nor was any statement racially
motivated. Further, the statements complained of would be subject to qualified
privilege. The Defence further states that Dr. Chohan has not suffered harm or
damages, and commenced the action as a manoeuver to gain advantage in an
ongoing interpersonal conflict with other physicians.

[
14
]

The Amended Statement of Defence
of Dr. Glen Baker denies any act of defamation or participation in a course of
action to defame and discredit Dr. Chohan. Any statements made were not
defamatory, nor racially motivated, nor the result of “politicking”. Insofar as
any statements complained of consisted of or implied expressions of opinion or
comments, they were fair and
bona fide
comments, made in good faith, and
were not made maliciously or recklessly without regard for the truth. The
alleged statements are subject to qualified privilege in that they were spoken
by Dr. Baker subject to a duty to disseminate the information to Dr. Block who
similarly had a duty to receive the information. It is denied that Dr. Chohan
suffered harm or damages.

The
Evidence

[
15
]

I will set out the evidence in this
matter in some detail, as the parties apparently viewed the entire detailed
context over a number of years as being of importance in assessing the alleged
defamatory remarks.

[
16
]

Dr. Chohan is 41 years old. By all
accounts, he is a good psychiatrist. He received his medical degree in 1992,
and completed a one year internship and four year psychiatry residency. He
worked with Dr. Sanderman between July 1996 and June 1997, and started working
at FACS in July 1997. At that time, it was operated by the Alberta Mental
Health Board (“AMHB”). Dr. Cadsky was the clinical coordinator of FACS for most
of the period from the time Dr. Chohan started working at FACS in 1997 until
he retired from clinical practice in August
2006. Dr. Brooks was the clinical director of Forensic Psychiatry at AHE. He
retired in August 2003. As clinical coordinator of FACS, Dr. Cadsky reported to
Dr. Dempsey (Acting Medical Director, AHE) through Dr. Brooks (Clinical
Director of Forensic Psychiatry, AHE) until mid-2003 and then through Dr.
Friend, appointed to that position after September 2004. Between mid-2003 and
September 2004 Dr. Cadsky reported directly to Dr. Dempsey who was acting
Forensic Clinical Director at the time.

[
17
]

In July 2001, Dr. Chohan applied for and
obtained a general psychiatry position at the Royal Alexandra Hospital (“RAH”)
which was then under the auspices of Capital Health. Dr. King had commended Dr.
Chohan to Dr. Block for that position. Dr. Chohan has gone from splitting his
time fairly evenly between FACS and RAH to a current split of around 35% of his
time at FACS and 65% at RAH. In order to supervise students at RAH, he needed
to be a member of the academic staff, and
he contacted Dr. Baker (Chair
of Department of Psychiatry, University of Alberta) in 2001 in that regard, and
was granted a clinical lecturer/academic appointment. Dr. Cadsky wrote a
favourable letter with respect to Dr. Chohan’s work in support of that application.

[
18
]

Dr. Cadsky worked as a practicing
psychiatrist at AHE from 1983. He became the first psychiatrist in the
out-patient clinic. He was the manager of FACS from 1989 until 1994 and was
then clinical coordinator at FACS until 2006, with the exception of the period
between 2001 and his reinstatement on March 31, 2003. Dr. Chohan noticed no
animosity toward himself on Dr. Cadsky’s part prior to that time.
Dr. Cadsky testified that as clinical
coordinator, he did not control who worked at FACS, nor did he do the regular
medical staff reviews, but he might be invited to provide input to the
reviewing body. Dr. King testified that Dr. Cadsky would have had a very
strong say in this respect.

[
19
]

Dr. Cadsky testified that he understood
Dr. Chohan to have a reputation (at least in part conveyed by Dr. Tweddle) for
being
prickly, difficult and
touchy. He understood Dr. Chohan had had some sort of problem with Dr. Bland
when he did not get a job he wanted. The evidence with respect to that incident
follows. However, clinically, he always had a very good reputation, and Dr.
Cadsky said that Dr. Chohan’s clinical work was always of a high standard.

[
20
]

In February 2000, Dr. Chohan
suddenly gave up his work on the inpatient unit and asked to work full-time in
the outpatient unit at FACS. Dr. Cadsky agreed. Dr. Cadsky did not know much
about what had happened on the inpatient unit, but subsequently learned there
had been some concerns about the way Dr. Chohan was dealing with nursing staff
and patients on Unit 3-2. When questioned about this by Dr. Brooks, Dr. Chohan “got into a snit” and walked out
of the inpatient unit and did not want to work there anymore. Dr. Cadsky
testified that Dr. Chohan developed a reputation because of this incident, and
others, as being “paranoid”. Dr. Cadsky testified that in his observation, Dr.
Chohan withdrew from social contact with his peers and other staff between 2000
and 2002.

[
21
]

Dr. Tweddle was acting
clinical director episodically from the 1980s. She was the staff psychiatrist
on Unit 3-1. When Dr. Chohan worked with her as a resident, she found him to be
quiet, competent, hard-working, and respectful. She had no difficulties or
disagreements with him, he accepted her being clinical head of the team, and
although he was not as chatty as some, he was a very competent resident. Unit
3-2 was closed for some time due to funding, and Dr. Chohan had done some work
after his residency on that Unit. When Unit 3-2 re-opened in 1999 after
reinstatement of funding, Dr. Chohan moved to Unit 3-2. Dr. Tweddle soon
started hearing rumblings about problems in Dr. Chohan’s dealings with nurses and the manager.
She tried to keep out of the situation. Early in 2000, she met Dr. Chohan in
the corridor and he was very angry and upset, storming down the corridor, and
he said he was leaving, he was furious, felt Dr. Brooks had not supported him
in a meeting, and was not working another day on the unit. She said she would
take over his patients if he looked after her outpatients until things got
sorted out. She subsequently crossed paths with him once a week at FACS.

[
22
]

Dr. Cadsky stated that w
hen Drs. Woods and Rai started at FACS,
he would have gone through the entire department staff in terms of their
strengths and weaknesses, and would have told them he kept his distance from
Dr. Chohan. However, he stated he would not have told them to stay away from
Dr. Chohan, as they would have had to deal with him in their work.

[
23
]

Dr. Cadsky was removed as clinical
coordinator because he called a Calgary psychiatrist, Dr. Hashman, a “greedy
money grubbing Jew”. Dr. Cadsky testified that he made this comment in
January 2000 to another physician in
private. He stated that he made the comment because Dr. Dusker had come up from
Calgary to help with the inpatient unit, and during a staff meeting, he
described how they did their billings in Calgary which apparently involved
charging the health care system up to seven 15 minute units for one hour of
work. Dr. Cadsky found this to be unethical, and he made the comment on the way
out of the meeting. Dr. Cadsky said he was angry at way they were misusing and
abusing the payment system. He used the word “greedy” due to the behavior discussed, and “Jew” because Dr.
Hashman wore a Jewish skull cap. Dr. Cadsky testified that the day prior to the
comments in question, his 14 year old daughter had been admitted to the
hospital with a tumour on her chest.

[
24
]

Dr. Dusker repeated this to Dr.
Hashman, and Dr. Hashman repeated it to several others and it ended up as a
formal complaint to head of forensic services, Dr. Brooks. Dr. Cadsky responded
to the complaint by writing an apology to Dr. Hashman and Dr. Levine, as the
complaint included Dr. Levine, who also said he was offended by the statement.
Dr. Cadsky acknowledged it was wrong to make the comment about Dr. Hashman’s
religion.

[
25
]

Two weeks later, Dr. Cadsky
received a call from Dr. Beausejour (chief medical officer of the AMHB), who
told him at a subsequent meeting in February 2001 that the apology had not been
accepted. It was not clear to Dr. Cadsky whether it was Dr. Hashman or Dr.
Beausejour who did not accept the apology. Dr. Cadsky asked what Dr. Beausejour
wanted, but he found the latter to be evasive. In May 2001, a memorandum was
distributed to all medical staff by Dr. Beausejour stating that Dr. Cadsky had
been dismissed from his position as clinical coordinator. Dr. Cadsky had not
heard anything from Dr. Beausejour between the meeting and the memorandum. He
had heard through the grapevine one week prior that “something big was coming
down”.

[
26
]

Dr. Tweddle testified that although the official reason given for
removing Dr. Cadsky as clinical director was the comment about Dr. Hashman, in
her view the real reason was an attempt by the senior administration to get
back at him and give a message to the medical staff because they had been
involved for a fairly long period of time in some quite acrimonious disputes
with the new acting medical director of the AMHB and the CEO.

[
27
]

Dr. Dempsey also testified regarding
difficulty between the psychiatrists and the AMHB as they moved toward the
transition with Capital Health.
She stated that after Dr. Cadsky took a stress leave in late
2002/early 2003, she became aware of complaints and bickering or infighting in
forensic program. She was acting medical director at AHE at the time. She
stated that she had never heard a negative word about Dr. Cadsky before; he had
single-handedly set up the forensics program which was well respected. She
also testified that to her knowledge, things were running smoothly at FACS
prior to April 2003, Dr. Brooks had general support and the program had a good
reputation.

[
28
]

Dr. Chohan and others at FACS signed a
letter dated May 18, 2001 to Dr. Beausejour, Acting Medical Director of Alberta
Hospital, stating that while they did not condone Dr. Cadsky’s statement about
Dr. Hashman, they believed the complaint was not handled appropriately, and a
private resolution would have been the most appropriate outcome.
Dr. Santana testified that Dr. Tweddle
asked him to ask Dr. Chohan to sign the letter, which Dr. Chohan did do.
Dr. Cadsky testified that he did not lobby for the letter.

[
29
]

Dr. Metelitsa moved
in 1995 from Russia to Calgary. He began working at FACS in 1996. Dr. Cadsky
assisted Dr. Metelitsa in settling in Edmonton.

[
30
]

Dr. Santana moved to
Edmonton from England in 2000 to work at FACS. Drs. Cadsky and Tweddle assisted
him with the move. He later also took a position as clinical associate
professor at the University of Alberta. He was initially offered a position at
FACS in 1999. At the time, he said he was interested in inpatient work, and
when he arrived Dr. Chohan had ceased working at Unit 3-2 (in the interim Dr.
Tweddle had provided in-patient care) and Dr. Santana took over. He testified
that he did not know why Dr. Chohan had left, but he gradually learned that Dr.
Chohan had had problems with “management interference” and felt that the clinical director (Dr.
Brooks) had not been supportive of his position. Dr. Santana left FACS in March
2, 2007 for general  psychiatry at AHE.

[
31
]

Dr. Santana stated that he had
very limited contact with Dr. Chohan from 1999 to 2001. He had been told Dr.
Chohan was very difficult and was not team player, so he never really talked
with him. However, he personally never found Dr. Chohan to be difficult. Dr.
Santana also testified that he was told by Dr. Tweddle that as soon as there
was a full complement of staff at FACS, Dr. Cadsky would make sure Dr. Chohan
left. Dr. Cadsky testified that he did not recall saying this to Dr. Tweddle. Dr.
Tweddle testified that she never heard Dr. Cadsky say he would force Dr. Chohan
to leave, nor did she ever hear that from anyone else. She was not aware of Dr.
Cadsky ever starting an argument with Dr. Chohan. She candidly testified that
Dr. Chohan had left places before, and it would have suited her if he had left,
as it was very difficult having him as a colleague.

[
32
]

Dr. Santana testified that when he
started having problems within the department, Dr. Chohan came to offer him
support, and said he and other psychiatrists had similar problems and not to
lose heart.

[
33
]

Dr. Woods, who graduated
from his psychiatry residency at the University of Alberta in 2002, testified
that while he was in his third year of residency working with Dr. Tweddle, he
asked Dr. Cadsky if there were any openings at FACS. Dr. Cadsky advised there
was nothing open, but it would not be difficult to raise the ire of Dr. Chohan
and then a position would be available. He acknowledged in cross-examination
that ultimately he was able to get a position at FACS in July 2002 without Dr.
Chohan leaving.

[
34
]

Dr. Rai arrived in
Canada in 2002 to work at FACS as a forensic psychiatrist. He testified that
Dr. Cadsky helped him get settled when he first arrived. Dr. Rai stated that
Dr. Cadsky had said during his orientation at FACS that Dr. Chohan was
deliberately sidelined as Dr. Cadsky perceived him to be difficult to work
with. This affected Dr. Rai’s interactions with Dr. Chohan, and he avoided him.

[
35
]

Dr. Rai explained that on February
4, 2003 he and Dr. Woods met with Dr. Cadsky at the latter’s house. Dr. Rai
testified that he and Dr. Woods went to see him primarily with respect to
happenings at FACS.
Dr. Woods testified it was primarily a social visit.
Mr. Reddick (administrator at FACS who dealt with non-medical staff, and who
was generally in charge of the program) was anxious to allocate specific responsibilities to Dr. Rai (violence
program) and Dr. Woods (sex offender program). Dr. Cadsky had been off work and
Dr. Rai wanted to run this by him. Dr. Rai knew Dr. Cadsky had been ill, and
that his daughter had recently died. The three shared some wine. Dr. Rai
testified that when discussing mental illness, Dr. Cadsky made inappropriate
remarks regarding Dr. Chohan, referring to him as a “paranoid Sikh”, and stating that he had plans to have
him removed from FACS in some way. Dr. Rai testified that Dr. Cadsky  said he
was planning to provoke some sort of argument with Dr. Chohan and he would
leave.

[
36
]

Dr. Rai found these comments
inappropriate, unprofessional, and demeaning. He took them seriously. The
comment caused Dr. Rai concern regarding his own interactions with Dr. Chohan.
He did not recall any other psychiatrist being discussed at that meeting. He
testified that he has never heard anyone but Dr. Cadsky say Dr. Chohan is
paranoid.

[
37
]

Dr. Woods testified that he was
not surprised at the comments, as he was already aware of Dr. Cadsky’s dislike
of Dr. Chohan, and was aware of a similar situation when Dr. Cadsky had
referred to another psychiatrist as a “greedy Jew”. Dr. Woods did not say
anything to Dr. Cadsky at the time of the comment.

[
38
]

Dr. Rai testified that there was
an amicable ending to the meeting at Dr. Cadsky’s house. Dr. Rai did not tell
Dr. Chohan about these comments right away as he thought it was a very
sensitive issue. However, he believed it needed to be dealt with as he thought
Dr. Chohan was at risk professionally at FACS for no good reason. He did know
how to “take it forward” at the time.

[
39
]

Dr. Rai testified that he did not
find Dr. Cadsky to be prejudiced or insulting to him when he helped Dr. Rai get
settled in Edmonton. Dr. Cadsky gave no indication that he was racist. He found
Dr. Cadsky’s statement that Dr. Chohan was a “paranoid Sikh” to be difficult to
reconcile with Dr. Cadsky’s behaviour.

[
40
]

Dr. Cadsky testified with respect
to the visit of Drs. Rai and Woods. They arrived together, and Dr. Rai was the
spokesman. He explained that one of the reasons for the visit was that the
manager was trying to institute changes with which they were not happy. The
three had a glass of wine in the family room. Dr. Cadsky said not to worry, and
he would speak to the manager when he got back. Dr. Cadsky then went on to
discuss what would happen in the department when Dr. Brooks left. Dr. Brooks
had talked about leaving for several years. As part of the discussion, Dr.
Cadsky went through each psychiatrist and gave his opinion regarding who should
be clinical director. He referred to the physicians with various epithets, for
example “English diva” (Dr. Tweddle), “narcissistic Spaniard” (Dr. Santana),
“disorganized Mexican” (Dr. Mejia), “paranoid Sikh” (Dr. Chohan), etc.  He
referred to Dr. Chohan in that way because Dr. Chohan had a reputation for
being paranoid and he was obviously Sikh. Dr. Cadsky testified that these
references were not malicious, and he got along extremely well with most of
them. He stated that he had no interest in Dr. Chohan’s race or religion, and
that he used the word “Sikh” simply because of his appearance.

[
41
]

Dr. Cadsky testified that Drs. Rai
and Woods did not express any shock or tell him not to use that type of
language. Nor did they say they would tell Dr. Chohan. Dr. Cadsky stated that
he viewed the discussion as a private conversation.

[
42
]

Dr. Cadsky testified that he would
not have said he would force Dr. Chohan to resign. However, he stated that Dr.
Chohan had a track record of getting into arguments with his bosses and
leaving, so he thought it was just a matter of time before it happened with Dr.
Cadsky. Dr. Cadsky testified that he treated Dr. Chohan with kid gloves and was
very careful of him. Dr. Cadsky testified that if he said anything, it would
have been that Dr. Chohan would probably get into a snit with Dr. Cadsky and resign.
He stated that he never tried to force a dispute with Dr. Chohan to get him to
resign. He further stated that he never had the power to dismiss any of the
psychiatrists.

[
43
]

Dr. Cadsky testified that by
referring to Dr. Chohan as “paranoid”, he had in mind seven characteristics of
paranoid personality disorder. In his view, four applied to Dr. Chohan as he:
1) was quick to perceive attacks on his character and quick to overreact or
fight back, 2) read demeaning or threatening messages into otherwise ordinary
comments, 3) bore grudges, and could not let go or forgive insults or slights,
and 4) believed others were out to harm him. He testified that by the time he
made the comments to Drs. Rai and Woods, he believed Dr. Chohan filled the
criteria for a clinical diagnosis of paranoid personality disorder. However, he
never had any concerns regarding Dr. Chohan’s clinical abilities as a
psychiatrist.

[
44
]

Dr. Cadsky stated that when in
public, he tries to put a damper on his political uncorrectness. He stated he
never made the “paranoid Sikh” comment to Dr. Chohan himself. He has called him
“paranoid” on other occasions, but did not recall having called him a “paranoid
Sikh” on any other occasion.

[
45
]

Dr. Tweddle, who has worked with
Dr. Cadsky for many years, testified that Dr. Cadsky is not racist or
malicious, although he can be big-footed, rude and obnoxious. She stated the he
is equally like that with everyone. She stated that he is not an easy person to
deal with. She stated that she too has never had any difficulty in private
conversation saying what she thinks about people.

[
46
]

Dr. Cadsky testified that in March
2003, he received a call from someone from the AMHB with respect to resolving a
lawsuit Dr. Cadsky had commenced over his termination as clinical coordinator.
Dr. Cadsky indicated that he would drop the lawsuit if his reinstatement were
part of the settlement, and he was in fact reinstated. He testified that his
duties did not significantly change during the time he was suspended from his position
as clinical coordinator.

[
47
]

Dr. Gardener, Chief Medical
Officer and Vice President of Capital Health, was consulted with respect to Dr.
Cadsky’s reinstatement. He consulted with Dr. White (regional program clinical
director of psychiatry for the region) and Eleanor Grant and was shown the
letter of May 18, 2001 that had been signed by at least the majority of the
doctors at FACS. As a result, he did not register any concerns with respect to
the reinstatement.

[
48
]

Dr. Dempsey was a member of the
AHE credentials committee and medical advisory committee (MAC) that made the
decision to reinstate Dr. Cadsky. Dr. Dempsey was consulted as acting medical
director, AHE sitting on both those committees. She testified that the reasons
why Dr. Cadsky was reinstated were complex: he had a previous excellent record;
at the time he made the comments he was under a very severe form of stress due
to his daughter’s diagnosis and subsequently death, and his myocardial
infarction; he had apologized to those involved; and he was not given due
process at the time he was dismissed (it would normally go through the
credentials committee and the MAC). When the recommendation went to Dr. Block
(Chief
Psychiatrist, RAH), he contacted
Dr. Gardener, who contacted Dr. Dempsey to discuss the reinstatement.

[
49
]

Dr. Santana testified regarding a
dispute with Dr. Tweddle, with whom he shared the rehabilitation department,
regarding a serious incident involving a patient in the community, which
resulted in a review. Dr. Santana testified that he was warned by a number of
people that Dr. Tweddle would be very critical of him in front of his team
during an upcoming serious incident review in March 2003. Dr. Santana cancelled
his attendance at the review that day. He sought the support of other psychiatrists.
Dr. Santana spoke to Dr. Cadsky about it and the latter said Dr. Tweddle had
overreacted, but since the serious incident took place in community, Dr.
Santana was not to worry, as it was his turf.

[
50
]

Dr. Tweddle testified regarding the
same matter. She stated that Dr. Santana had an outpatient who had been her
outpatient from Unit 3-2. This woman had threatened to kill Dr. Tweddle. Dr.
Tweddle heard the woman was deteriorating. A community nurse became spooked on
a visit to the patient, and arrangements were made for police and male staff to
attend at her apartment. The patient attacked the policeman with an axe, and
said she had contemplated attacking the nurse with the axe, and talked about
having Dr. Tweddle and the nurse killed. Dr. Santana had reduced her medication
prior to this incident. Dr. Tweddle testified that serious incident reviews are
not intended to lay blame, but for everybody involved to learn from each other
and to try to avoid similar problems in the future. Dr. Tweddle intended to go
because she felt she was involved in the case, but found out from Dr. Brooks
that Dr. Santana thought she was attacking him, and she decided not to go.
Shortly thereafter, Dr. Santana came storming into her office, and told her he
was no longer prepared to cover her patients as he had agreed to do for her
upcoming vacation, because she would blame him for any problems. Since that
time, she has not had a good relationship with Dr. Santana. She found the
situation to be very upsetting.

[
51
]

In April 2003, Dr. Rai received a
letter saying Dr. Cadsky had been reinstated. This prompted him to go to Dr.
Chohan about Dr. Cadsky’s comments. He told Dr. Chohan to keep the information
confidential. Dr. Rai did not want to be involved, having only been at FACS for
six months. He had a special licence requiring renewal every 2½ years, which
was dependent on satisfactory performance and the position not being filled by
a Canadian physician. He was accountable to Dr. Cadsky, and his appraisals
would go through Dr. Cadsky. He felt he was in a relatively weak position in
his job given his temporary licence. He needed time to work through whether he
wanted to get involved.

[
52
]

Dr. Chohan testified that he went on vacation to India in March 2003,

Analysis

[
239
]

Dr.
Chohan alleges that Defendants made various defamatory comments, and that the
defamation of the Defendants was used to discredit and dismiss his concerns
regarding racism, discrimination and harassment in the workplace.

[
240
]

The parties agree that there are
three elements to the tort of defamation:

(a)        the words complained of are
defamatory;

(b)        the words complained of
refer to the plaintiff; and

(c)        the words complained of were
published to a third person.

[
241
]

As noted by R.E. Brown in
The
Law of Defamation in Canada
, 2nd ed. (Toronto, Ont.: Carswell, 1994‑)
at p. 1-31, a publication is considered defamatory if it has the tendency to
lower a person’s reputation in the estimation of reasonable persons in the
community.

[
242
]

The defences to a defamation
action include:

(a)        truth or justification;

(b)        consent to the publication;

(c)        absolute privilege;

(d)        qualified privilege;

(e)        protected reports; and

(f)        fair comment.

[
243
]

I will deal with the various
allegations in turn.

Dr.
Cadsky

[
244
]

Dr. Cadsky testified quite
candidly that he referred to Dr. Chohan as a “paranoid Sikh” in his home in a
discussion with Drs. Rai and Woods.

[
245
]

The evidence is less clear with
respect to the alleged statement that Dr. Cadsky intended to force Dr. Chohan
to resign from his position with FACS. I find on the evidence that Dr. Cadsky
did not state that he would force Dr. Chohan to resign. I found Dr. Cadsky to
be a straightforward witness with strong views, who did not tailor his evidence
in order to protect himself. I find on the entirety of the evidence that he
likely stated something to the effect that it would not take much for Dr.
Chohan to leave FACS, given his reputation for being somewhat hot-headed and
for quitting positions over disagreements, and I further find that reputation
was supported by the evidence, for example his departure from Unit 3-2. I also
find that Dr. Cadsky may have repeated words to this effect on other occasions.

[
246
]

With respect to the “paranoid
Sikh” comment, Brown,
supra
states at p. 1-32 that a statement will not
be actionable as defamatory unless it is reasonably understood in a defamatory
sense by those to whom it is published. The courts consider any reasonable
implication the words may bear, the context in which they were spoken, the
audience to whom they were published, and the manner in which they were
presented. I accept that Drs. Rai and Woods reasonably understood the statement
in a defamatory sense. All three persons present were psychiatrists on whom the
potential significance of the characterization of “paranoid” would not be lost,
the discussions involved the workplace, and there is no suggestion the comment
was not meant to be taken seriously.

[
247
]

Counsel for Dr. Cadsky suggests
that the comment was merely insulting; intemperate language was the order of
the day at FACS, and many of the medical staff reveled in devising abusive
epithets and bandying them about. There is no doubt that a culture of
disrespect developed among a number of individuals at FACS. Obviously, Dr. Cadsky’s
statement was insulting. In my view, the fact that other insulting or
defamatory comments might have been made by other individuals at FACS about
other physicians is of limited relevance in this case in determining whether
the “paranoid Sikh” statement was defamatory.

[
248
]

I find that Dr. Cadsky’s reference to Dr. Chohan as
being a “Sikh” was not racially motivated and was not intended to be defamatory
.
There was ample evidence that Dr. Cadsky was very generous and accommodating to
persons of all races. In some ways, his verbal rhetoric was very much out of
keeping with his actions. Dr. Chohan himself testified that being called a Sikh
does not bother him, and that he is proud of his faith, although this was one
of the grounds for his human rights complaint. There was no evidence that Dr.
Cadsky’s reference to Dr. Chohan as “paranoid” was somehow tied to his
reference to Dr. Chohan’s faith, nor did Drs. Rai and Woods testify that they
understood it in this way.

[
249
]

As for the comment that Dr. Chohan
was “paranoid”, the evidence was that this statement was intended to and was
understood as a comment on Dr. Chohan’s mental state. There was a considerable
amount of time spent discussing the various ways of understanding the term
“paranoid”. I accept that it can cover a wide range of meaning. At one end of
the spectrum it can be a colloquial  shorthand for a person exhibiting some
minimal suspicion or fearfulness; at the other end, it can signify a
personality disorder or, in the extreme, fixed delusional thinking. All of the
individuals present at the time the statement was made are highly trained
psychiatrists. Dr. Cadsky’s evidence was that he intended the term to be
understood in its clinical sense. It was certainly understood by Dr. Chohan to
be a serious comment on his mental health, and in my view Drs. Rai and Woods
also reasonably understood it to be such a comment.

[
250
]

It
is not disputed that the remark was published to someone other than the subject
of the remark, in this case Drs. Rai and Woods. I find that the statement was
repeated by Dr. Rai in his letter to Dr. Gardener, and to individuals involved
in the processes established by Dr. Gardener in an attempt to deal with the
problems at FACS. Dr. Chohan himself repeated the statement to a number of
individuals in order to garner support.

[
251
]

Dr. Cadsky submits that the
comment was not made maliciously or recklessly without regard for the truth.
Dr. Cadsky further pleads truth or justification, qualified privilege and fair
comment.

[
252
]

Dr. Cadsky testified that in his
view, Dr. Chohan met four of the seven criteria associated with a paranoid
personality in that he:
1)
was quick to perceive attacks on his character and quick to overreact or fight
back, 2) read demeaning or threatening messages into otherwise ordinary
comments, 3) bore grudges, and could not let go or forgive insults or slights,
and 4) believed others were out to harm him. He testified that by the time he
made the comments to Drs. Rai and Woods, he believed Dr. Chohan filled the
criteria for a clinical diagnosis of paranoid personality disorder. However, he
never had any concerns regarding Dr. Chohan’s clinical abilities. I conclude from his
evidence that Dr. Cadsky intended to convey that he viewed Dr. Chohan as having
some paranoid personality traits, but not the type of paranoid psychosis which
it was agreed on the evidence would render him unfit to continue in the
practice of psychiatry.

[
253
]

Dr. Cadsky’s professional opinion was not directly
challenged.
Dr. Chohan himself testified that he was proud and held a
system of belief which included fighting “to the end” for justice. The evidence
certainly supports Dr. Cadsky’s view that Dr. Chohan was not quick to overlook
wrongs.

[
254
]

One does not need a
degree in psychiatry to observe that the indicia referred to by Dr. Cadsky are
exhibited on occasion by persons of sound mental health. It is
interesting to note that the characteristics relied on by Dr. Cadsky were
viewed by Dr. Chohan’s colleagues and acquaintances in varying ways: Dr. King
and other members of the group of seven admired Dr. Chohan’s dedication,
perseverance and insistence on pursuing justice, while other professionals such
as Drs. Baker and Ohlhauser were genuinely alarmed at the strength of Dr. Chohan’s
convictions and the single-mindedness with which he pursued a resolution which
would meet his exacting standards. Others found his style simply irritating and
offensive - to them, he was a “thorn in the flesh”.

[
255
]

It is neither necessary nor
possible in this case for this Court to pronounce upon the correctness of Dr.
Cadsky’s professional opinion. Clearly, equally able psychiatrists may
reasonably disagree on the significance of certain behaviours. I do note,
however, that other highly trained individuals independently experienced
concerns that Dr. Chohan may have been in a fragile mental state based on the
same type of behaviour that Dr. Cadsky concluded indicated he was exhibiting
some of the criteria of a paranoid personality disorder. I am satisfied that
Dr. Cadsky honestly believed that Dr. Chohan had at certain times exhibited
certain traits (as do a number of us, no doubt) which were in keeping with the
profile of a paranoid personality. Neither that professional opinion nor the
sincerity with which it was held, was undermined by the Plaintiff’s evidence.

[
256
]

With respect to the assertion of
a qualified privilege, I find on the evidence that Drs. Rai and Woods attended
at Dr. Cadsky’s home to seek his advice or input on various happenings at FACS.
While there may have been a social component to the visit, the primary topic of
discussion appears to have been politics at FACS. I find that the conversation
turned to the leadership vacuum and the pending resignation of Dr. Brooks. I
further find that Drs. Rai and Woods had an interest in receiving Dr. Cadsky’s
views on the eligibility of various psychiatrists at FACS to fill leadership
roles. While there was no evidence that they directly solicited his comments in
this regard, there was also no evidence that they did not willingly participate
in the discussion of the strengths and weaknesses of various psychiatrists at
FACS.

[
257
]

An occasion is privileged if a
statement is fairly made by a person in the discharge of some public or private
duty, or for the purpose of protecting some private interest, if it is made to
a person who has some corresponding interest in receiving it. The test is
whether persons of ordinary intelligence and moral principle, or the great
majority of right-minded persons, would have considered it a duty to
communicate the information to those to whom it was published: Brown,
supra
,
at p. 13-4.

[
258
]

Further, as was stated by Lord
Nicholls of Birkenhead in
Reynolds v. Times Newspapers Ltd.
,

[1999] 4 All E.R. 609
at 615 (H.L.)
:

There are occasions when the person to whom a
statement is made has a special interest in learning the honestly held views of
another person, even if those views are defamatory of someone else and cannot
be proved to be true. When the interest is of sufficient importance to outweigh
the need to protect reputation, the occasion is regarded as privileged.

[
259
]

It is not necessary that the facts
of the particular communication should be of interest to the public at large or
beneficial to the public interest, but only that the appropriate part of the
public had an interest in the subject matter: see Brown,
supra
at 13-15
and cases cited therein.

[
260
]

I find that Dr. Cadsky
communicated what were in his view Dr. Chohan’s personality frailties with a
view to discussing who might best fill the leadership role at FACS.  I further
find that he reasonably felt he had a duty, as the senior psychiatrist who had
developed the program at FACS over several decades and who viewed his ongoing
involvement at that point as being limited to several more years, to speak out
with respect to the eligibility of various potential leadership candidates.
This “duty” correlated to the interests of his audience. There is no doubt that
Drs. Rai and Woods, both at the start of what might be presumed to be lengthy
careers in forensic psychiatry at FACS, had an avid interest in the future
leadership of FACS. In my view, a reasonable person in such circumstances
should as a matter of public policy be free to speak as did Dr. Cadsky. I find
that the occasion was privileged.

[
261
]

Furthermore, I find that there was no malice in Dr.
Cadsky’s statement. Malice encompasses spite or ill will towards someone, or
any indirect motive or ulterior purpose other than the sense of duty or the
mutual interest which the privileged occasion created:
Leenan v. Canadian
Broadcasting Corp.
,
2000 CanLII 22380 (ON SC)
,
[2000] O.J. No. 1359
at para.
140
(S.C.J.)
.
Although the circumstances
in
Cimolai v. Hall
,
[2007] B.C.J. No.
810
,
2007 BCCA 225
were somewhat different, the decisions at both levels in
that case are instructive with respect to qualified privilege and malice, both
Courts confirming that dislike is not the equivalent of malice.

[
262
]

Dr. Cadsky came across in testimony as very abrupt,
blatantly expressing his strongly held opinions with no attempt to soften or
nuance his statements. This, not unlike Dr. Chohan’s strength of conviction,
could be perceived by some as a character flaw. However, I also found him to be
pragmatic and fair in that he adamantly stated that Dr. Chohan was an excellent
physician whom he had supported in a number of ways in his career. Dr. Cadsky
testified that his reference to Dr. Chohan as “paranoid” was an expression of
fact based on his observations. That it was insulting does not make it
malicious.
I find that the statement he made to Drs. Rai and Woods was
not malicious, but was conveyed in the context of a frank discussion of the
leadership qualities (or lack thereof) of various individuals in anticipation
of a leadership vacuum.

[
263
]

Although not overly relevant, I
feel compelled to comment on the actions of Drs. Rai and Woods. I have no doubt
that Dr. Cadsky’s comments in the usual course might give rise to some
legitimate concern for their colleague, Dr. Chohan, particularly in the event
of Dr. Cadsky’s subsequent reinstatement. However, it is difficult to
understand their thinking in engaging in a discussion with a colleague who had
so recently experienced in such rapid succession some of the most significant
life traumas imaginable, and then turning around and sharing certain statements
with those for whom the communication was clearly not intended. Although Dr.
Rai cited professional security as his main reason for withholding this
information from a broader public, I cannot but hope that Dr. Cadsky’s very
unfortunate personal situation was at least one of his underlying concerns.
When the comment was shared, it predictably fanned the flames and fueled the
resistance to Dr. Cadsky’s reinstatement, and in that sense became one weapon among
a number of others in the power struggle at FACS.

[
264
]

I should not be understood as
condoning the use of such intemperate language as was used by Dr. Cadsky. There
were undoubtedly other ways for Dr. Cadsky to express his personal views which
would not have been nearly so offensive, particularly to a fellow psychiatrist.
Dr. Cadsky was, not surprisingly, disciplined for his provocative, insulting
and categorical language.

Dr.
Gardener and Capital Health

[
265
]

Dr. Gardener’s involvement arose at
the instigation of the group of seven. The Plaintiff alleges that Dr. Gardener
made a defamatory statement to Dr. Block when he phoned him and expressed
concerns about Dr. Chohan. This was after Capital Health had taken over.

[
266
]

At the time of the subject phone call, Dr. Gardener
had received credible expressions of concern from Drs. Baker and Ohlhauser. Dr.
Ohlhauser’s concerns arose not only from his own interactions with Dr. Chohan,
but also as a result of communications of concern by Dr. King, a self-described
admirer and ally of Dr. Chohan. Dr. King had also called Dr. Gardener’s office
in his absence to express his concerns.

[
267
]

I find on the evidence that
although Dr. Chohan may have apprised Dr. Gardener early on in a general way of
concerns of discrimination and intimidation, Dr. Gardener had no knowledge of
the “paranoid Sikh” comment when he phoned Dr. Block. The basis for Dr.
Gardener’s concern was not Dr. Cadsky’s opinion that Dr. Chohan exhibited
certain paranoid behaviors. Rather, it was information provided by two persons
who were not involved in the  political turmoil at FACS, and by another one who
identified himself with the unhappy group of seven of which Dr. Chohan was a
part.

[
268
]

Dr. King testified of the group of seven: “we were all
paranoid”.
Dr. Chohan testified to his own considerable frustration at
the difficulty he had in convincing persons in positions of authority that
discrimination and intimidation were occurring at FACS. At one point, he
conceded that these difficulties made him “paranoid”. In my view, a
considerable contributing factor to his distress was his inability to relate
the details of what Dr. Cadsky had purportedly said to Drs. Rai and Woods, due
to Dr. Rai’s desire to keep the matter confidential.

[
269
]

I find that Dr. Gardener, given
his role and the information he had been provided, had a clear duty to
ascertain whether the concerns raised to him posed any problem in terms of Dr.
Chohan’s clinical practice and personal welfare. He knew the situation at FACS
was complicated by the factions which had developed, and chose to contact Dr.
Block, Dr. Chohan’s colleague from a setting out of which there had apparently
come no reports of conflict implicating Dr. Chohan. This was an entirely
reasonable manner of fulfilling his duty, and was eminently fair to Dr. Chohan,
as Dr. Block was not partisan with anyone at FACS. Dr. Block had an interest in
hearing the concerns of Dr. Gardener, as he too would have a duty to ensure, as
concerns were raised, that Dr. Chohan’s practice was not adversely affected by
any stressors. Dr. Gardener’s communications with Dr. Block satisfied him that
Dr. Chohan’s anger over the situation at FACS was not adversely affecting his
ability to practice his profession.  No steps were ever taken to restrict Dr. Chohan’s
clinical practice in any way.

[
270
]

Assuming that Dr. Gardener’s communication can be
characterized as defamatory, I find that the occasion of this communication was
subject to qualified privilege.
Further, I find that there was absolutely
no evidence from which any malice could be inferred on the part of Dr.
Gardener.

[
271
]

Dr. Chohan alleges in the
Statement of Claim that because of Dr. Gardener’s relationship with Capital
Health, he acted as its employee or agent and therefore Capital Health is
vicariously liable for Dr. Gardener’s defamation. As I have found no liability
on the part of Dr. Gardener in his personal capacity, there is no vicarious
liability on the part of Capital Health.

Dr.
Baker

[
272
]

The Plaintiff alleges that Dr. Baker made a defamatory
statement to Dr. Block when he phoned him and expressed concerns about Dr.
Chohan.

[
273
]

Dr. Baker had been apprised of the
situation at FACS, and the general concerns of discrimination and intimidation
prior to calling Dr. Block. Following Dr. King’s call to Dr. Gardener’s office,
and Eleanor Grant’s subsequent call to Dr. Dempsey, the latter spoke with Dr.
Baker. Although Dr. Baker did not recall this discussion, I am satisfied on the
basis of the documentation adduced at trial that it did occur.

[
274
]

Dr. Baker had also met personally with Dr. Chohan on
another matter and became quite concerned about him. Again, it may be that Dr.
Chohan’s expression of his anger was heightened  at his frustration in not
being able to reveal the details of the particular incident concerning himself.
In Dr. Baker’s
subsequent discussions with Dr. Ohlhauser, his concerns
were bolstered.

[
275
]

These communications led Dr. Baker
to contact Dr. Block, again to obtain some input from a disinterested third
party as to Dr. Chohan’s state. As with the communication by Dr. Gardener, I am
satisfied that Dr. Baker was genuinely concerned about a colleague in distress,
based in large part on his own observations which were not seriously questioned
at trial, and that he wished to ensure that Dr. Chohan was functioning well in
spite of his anger, and was receiving the support of colleagues outside of the
political morass at FACS.

[
276
]

I find that Dr. Baker’s
communication was not defamatory. I accept his evidence that what he
communicated was concern over the extent of Dr. Chohan’s anger which he had
personally observed, and that he would not have used the term “paranoid” to
describe another physician.

[
277
]

Dr. Baker had an interest as a
fellow physician in ensuring that Dr. Chohan was not unduly distressed, and Dr.
Block had an interest in receiving the communication and was a person who would
be able to comment in an objective way on Dr. Chohan’s state. Therefore, even
if the content of the communication was defamatory, I find that it took place on
an occasion of qualified privilege and I am satisfied that malice played no
part in Dr. Baker’s decision to contact Dr. Block.

Dr. Ohlhauser

[
278
]

The Plaintiff alleges that Dr.
Ohlhauser defamed him when he contacted Dr. Hibbard and left a voice mail
message stating, “We have a sick doc here, can you call”, and when he left a
further voice mail message stating that he was concerned that Dr. Chohan was
paranoid.

[
279
]

I accept Dr. Ohlhauser’s evidence
that he would have said, “We
may
have a sick doc here...”. The nature of
his call was for the purpose of inquiring as to Dr. Chohan’s mental state, and
therefore it is reasonable to infer that he had not reached a conclusion at
that point in time. Drs. Ohlhauser and Chadsey both discussed the term of art
“sick doc” and I am satisfied that the phrase was used by them in their roles
at the College generally to refer to physicians in personal distress. The
distress may vary in degree and may have one or more of a number of sources. As
a result, in this context that statement without any further detail is so
ambiguous as to be almost meaningless.

[
280
]

The expression of concern that Dr. Chohan might be
paranoid arose out of Dr. King’s expression of concern to Dr. Ohlhauser about
his friend, Dr. Chohan, and discussions Dr. Ohlhauser had with Dr. Chohan when
he met with him personally. Again, the evidence is that Dr. Chohan was very
frustrated at the time not only with the situation at FACS, but with his
inability to impress upon those in authority the seriousness of his concerns,
which I attribute in large part to the fact that he did not feel at liberty to
relate his very specific example of what he viewed as discrimination and
intimidation by Dr. Cadsky.
I
find that it was not until September 2003 that Dr. Ohlhauser became aware of
Dr. Cadsky’s specific comments about Dr. Chohan through Dr. Rai.

[
281
]

Dr. Ohlhauser, at the time he called Dr. Hibbard, had
been asked by Dr. King to become involved in assisting Dr. Chohan to move
forward.
He had considerable experience, as Registrar and conflict
resolution consultant, in dealing with physicians in distress. Dr. Ohlhauser
would have been well aware of the ethical implications of ignoring possible
warning signs of stress on the part of physicians. Dr. King had urged him to take
on Dr. Chohan’s cause and give him some reassurance.

[
282
]

I find Dr. Ohlhauser’s comments, if they were
defamatory, were communicated on an occasion of qualified privilege.
At
the time he phoned Dr. Hibbard, he had an interest as a fellow physician and as
someone with a potential involvement in resolving some of the difficulties at
FACS, in ensuring that Dr. Chohan was not adversely affected by the situation
at FACS and his own reaction to it, and that Dr. Chohan had support from
persons outside of FACS. Dr. Hibbard, as a colleague of Dr. Chohan, had an
interest in receiving the communication, and was well positioned to comment on
his observations of Dr. Chohan in a more neutral setting. I find no direct
evidence, nor can I infer, any malice toward Dr. Chohan on the part of Dr.
Ohlhauser.

[
283
]

The Plaintiff also alleges that
Dr. Ohlhauser defamed him in his contacts in early July 2003 with Dr. Gardener
and Dr. Baker. These contacts flowed from Dr. King’s call to Dr. Gardener’s
office in his absence which resulted in the involvement of Dr. Baker, and his
appeal to Dr. Ohlhauser to help his friend, Dr. Chohan. Dr. Baker testified
that he contacted Dr. Ohlhauser after meeting with Dr. Chohan to see whether
Dr. Ohlhauser had similar concerns on observing Dr. Chohan’s reaction. Dr.
Ohlhauser contacted Dr. Gardener with respect to his concerns. He had no
official mandate at the time, and any official involvement in resolving issues
at FACS would have to have been authorized through Dr. Gardener. Again, for the
reasons given with respect to the other communications of Drs. Ohlhauser,
Gardener and Baker, I find that these communications occurred on an occasion of
qualified privilege and that they were not malicious.

[
284
]

The defence of fair comment was
also raised on the part of the Defendants. Some authorities treat fair comment
as an example of qualified privilege, although others distinguish the two. In
my view, there is an aspect of public interest with respect to the concerns
expressed by Drs. Ohlhauser, Gardener and Baker. I find that each of them was genuinely
concerned for Dr. Chohan’s well being as a professional colleague. However,
they also wished to ensure through their inquiries that Dr. Chohan’s anger was
not affecting his clinical practice. This public aspect may bring the inquiries
within the parameters of fair comment. However, given the evidence in this
case, in my view the communications are more appropriately analyzed through the
paradigm of qualified privilege.

Conclusion
on Liability

[
285
]

The events outlined above were
very unfortunate in many respects. I have found that none of the claims of
defamation have been made out. However, my analysis of the legal question of
defamation does not negate my finding that Dr. Chohan was justified in feeling
insulted and humiliated by having his mental integrity questioned. His
considerable frustration at his inability to convince those in authority of the
validity of his complaints is understandable. Unfortunately, the level of
frustration demonstrated by him was perceived as excessive by those who did not
know of Dr. Cadsky’s comment and his suppression of it out of respect for Dr.
Rai.

[
286
]

At the same time, Dr. Chohan appears to have been
consumed with his frustration to the point that he has, at times,
been
unable to put himself in the shoes of others who harboured no ill feelings
toward him and were attempting to make sense of the situation with limited
information. It is not surprising that his personal concerns about
discrimination and intimidation were not addressed in any concrete way before
the details of Dr. Cadsky’s comments were generally made known to the various
players in this saga. Further, it is true that expressions of concern can
sometimes mask ill will or be used to undermine the credibility of others.
However, it is equally true that expressions of concern can be genuinely
intended to ultimately support an individual in succeeding and overcoming
personal difficulties as well as obstacles posed by others. I am satisfied, on
the basis of the evidence before the Court, that the actions of Drs. Gardener,
Baker and Ohlhauser were in no way meant to undermine Dr. Chohan, and that he
would have understood them to be potential allies or at least neutral actors,
had he not been so frustrated in his attempts to communicate Dr. Cadsky’s
comments, and so dismissive and distrustful of anyone who expressed any level
of concern over his well being.

Damages

[
287
]

The
Plaintiff conceded prior to trial that the claim with respect to damages only
relates to damages on account of loss of reputation and that no special damages
such as loss of income are being claimed.

[
288
]

The Plaintiff cites
Hill v. Church of
Scientology of Toronto
,
1995 CanLII 59 (SCC)
,
[1995] 2 S.C.R. 1130
for the proposition that
general damages are presumed in defamation cases (see also
ss. 2(2)
of the
Defamation
Act
, R.S.A. 2000, c. D‑7) and there is no cap on general damages for
defamation.

[
289
]

Brown,
supra
states at
25-2:

In assessing damages the court may consider the
character and conduct of both the plaintiff and the defendant, together with
the nature and character of the defamatory publication, the extent of its
circulation and the circumstances under which it was made. Only those damages
may be recovered which flow naturally and directly from the defendant’s conduct
and for which he or she is the proximate cause. [...] Where the plaintiff’s
reputation is relatively unaffected, or the actions of the defendant are
innocent and the damages suffered insignificant, the court or jury is free to
award a nominal sum in damages.

[
290
]

Had any of the claims of defamation
been made out, any damages would have been nominal at best. There was no
evidence of any damage to Dr. Chohan’s professional reputation. He continues to
be held in the highest esteem with respect to his clinical practice, and he
freely admitted that his practice continued virtually without interruption
during the entire time period canvassed in the evidence, and even to the
present time.

[
291
]

Mr.
Saluja’s evidence was that Dr. Chohan also continues to be held in the highest
esteem by the Sikh community, and they wish for and look forward to a renewal
of his active participation in the community.

[
292
]

There was certainly evidence that
Dr. Chohan experienced distress over Dr. Cadsky’s comment. However, as I have
already stated, in my view his distress was only partly attributable to the
comment itself.
He became
exasperated at what he perceived as the unwillingness of those in authority to
take Dr. Cadsky to task for his comment. Had he been free to communicate his
specific concern earlier on, I am satisfied that he would have experienced much
less distress. To a considerable extent, in my view, his frustration
arose as a result of not feeling at liberty to relate the specifics of Dr.
Cadsky’s comment to those in positions of authority so that it could be
addressed in a tangible way, and in his reluctance to accept genuine
expressions of concern.

[
293
]

As has undoubtedly become
apparent, in my view this trial was unnecessarily long. Relatively little of
the evidence cited above was essential to the conclusions reached herein, and
most facts were not seriously in dispute, or in dispute at all.

[
294
]

Much of the evidence concerned the power struggle at FACS. Power
struggles go on all the time in the administrations of various organizations.
They are often acrimonious and can easily result in very polarized positions
and a certain demonizing of those holding different views. However, power
struggles do not, in themselves, give rise to a cause of action. Persons in positions of leadership are
routinely faced with difficult decisions, and may become unpopular for taking
certain positions. In this case, the power struggle at FACS provided the
backdrop for the impugned statements. In the end, much of the detailed evidence
in that regard was of limited relevance to the claims of defamation. In my
view, this litigation served largely as a forum for a litany of complaints
against the “old guard”, including complaints of discrimination,
intimidation, harassment, mismanagement and lack of effective leadership.

[
295
]

If I had found that defamation had
been made out against all or any of the Defendants, I would have awarded
nominal damages in the amount of $5,000.
